Dear Dr Emi Tanaka,

Thank you for handling the second round of our submission, and our thanks to the referee for a second careful report. The referee checked the package against the manuscript in detail, and the three comments were all correct. We confirmed each of them against the reviewed commits before changing anything, and the supplementary scripts made that much quicker.

This document reproduces each comment in full, followed by our response. Section numbers refer to the revised manuscript, and line numbers in the comments refer to the commits the referee reviewed (manuscript `4aa2c96`, package `bbc10d6`). The changes to the package are in the development version on GitHub (<https://github.com/pedreirajr/cnefetools>) and will be released on CRAN as version 0.4.0. That release will match the revised manuscript.

# Scope of the changes in this round

Comment 1 led to more code than a minor revision usually needs, so we explain the reasons for it before the point-by-point responses.

The referee asks for "a reliable way for users to handle shared border cells when combining municipal results". We could have documented how to merge the outputs of separate calls. But in the first round, Referee 2 had already pointed to the single-municipality scope as a significant limitation (R2.5), and our own Section 6 listed grids and polygon layers not restricted to municipal boundaries as a priority for future work. Documenting a merge procedure would have meant publishing a workaround for a limitation we had already promised to remove. So we removed it instead. All four analytical functions now take a vector of municipality codes and handle the shared cells themselves. The manuscript and version 0.4.0 describe the same interface, so the paper won't be out of date when it's published.

Apart from the change of boundaries described below, a call with a single code gives the same result as before. With a vector, the functions pool the addresses of all the municipalities before computing anything. To make this practical without downloading whole states, the package now reads the municipal boundaries and the census tracts it needs straight from its GitHub releases, through DuckDB's `httpfs` extension, and caches them by municipality. Two new arguments, `scope` and `p_target`, let users choose which addresses enter the cells along the outer edge of the region and which baseline the Balance Index and the BGBI use. The functions also report a few situations they used to handle silently: addresses whose H3 cell falls outside the grid, repeated features in `polygon`, and overlapping polygons.

Since the code changed, we ran the Section 5 benchmark again on the current version, with the same harness, machine and replicates, and the section now reports those numbers. The conclusions are unchanged.

Some of these changes also correct statements we made in the first-round response. We list them in the last section of this document.

# Comment 1: Correct the instructions for combining municipalities

> Section 6, p. 17 (manuscript source lines 1461–1470), says a border cell "belongs to exactly one of the two municipalities". However, `R/build_h3_grid.R` adds intersecting neighbours to the centre-selected cells. The same H3 identifier can therefore occur in both outputs, carrying different municipal contributions. A controlled example using synthetic adjacent boundaries and records through the real exported functions found 15 shared identifiers, 12 with nonzero counts on both sides, on both backends. The minimal supplementary script `reproduce_h3_border_cells.R` demonstrates the shared cell identifiers directly with the real grid builder and two adjacent rectangles; it needs no mocks or data downloads and does not repeat the counts/index checks.
>
> This matters because removing repeated `id_hex` rows can discard one municipality's contribution, while averaging separately calculated indices can give an incorrect regional result. For example, a shared cell with 20 private-household records from one municipality and 51 other-use records from the other has a residential share of `20 / 71 = 0.282`; averaging the separate shares gives 0.5. Repeated cell identifiers alone do not mean the underlying address records are duplicated.
>
> Please correct the exclusive-cell claim and choose and document a reliable way for users to handle shared border cells when combining municipal results. The guidance should explain how both municipalities' contributions are preserved, distinguish counts and additive totals from indices and averages, and address the different municipal reference values used by Balance and BGBI. The implementation is for the authors to decide. A short tested example would help users follow the supported approach and avoid incorrect regional results.

**Response:** **Accepted. The claim is removed, and the supported approach is now a single call with a vector of municipality codes.**

The referee is right, and the sentence was already wrong when we wrote it. Since version 0.2.3, from March 2026, the package adds the neighboring cells that intersect the boundary to the grid, so a cell on a shared border has appeared in the grids of both municipalities ever since. The sentence we added in the first round described the earlier rule, based on the cell center alone. Presenting the loop over municipalities as the way to combine them was also a mistake, for the reasons the referee gives.

`cnefe_counts()`, `compute_lumi()`, `tracts_to_h3()` and `tracts_to_polygon()` now accept a vector in `code_muni`. The addresses of all the municipalities are read as one table, and the H3 grid is built over the union of their boundaries, so every cell appears once. A cell on a shared border holds the addresses of both municipalities, and its indices are computed from those pooled counts. In the referee's example, the shared cell gets a residential share of 20 / 71, not 0.5. The same applies to the dasymetric interpolation, where a border cell receives the allocations of the tracts on both sides.

With polygons, `code_muni` doesn't even have to be given. In `cnefe_counts()`, `compute_lumi()` and `tracts_to_polygon()`, it can be left out with `scope = "geom"`, and the package then finds the municipalities that the polygons intersect, using the 2022 IBGE boundaries, and lists them in a message. A polygon layer that spans several municipalities can therefore be used directly, without the user working out which municipalities it covers. Only the H3 grid always needs `code_muni`, since it's built from the boundaries of those municipalities.

On the points the referee asks the guidance to cover:

- **Counts and additive totals against indices and averages.** Counts from separate calls can still be summed by `id_hex` to recover the pooled values, while indices and averages can't, since they are ratios of counts. The help page of each function has a "Several municipalities" section that says this.
- **The reference value of the Balance Index and the BGBI.** With several codes, $P$ is the residential share of the region as a whole, so `bal` and `bgbi` are measured against the region, not against each municipality, and adding a municipality to `code_muni` changes them in every cell. The documentation says that indices from separate calls aren't comparable with each other, nor with a regional call, because each call has its own $P$. Users who want a baseline that doesn't depend on the set of municipalities can pass `p_target`, a fixed residential share such as one set by a land use plan. That's the extension proposed in the conclusions of Pedreira Junior et al. (2026).
- **The outer edge of the region.** Cells along the outer edge of the region also intersect municipalities that were not requested. By default (`scope = "muni"`) they hold only the addresses of the requested municipalities, which is the behavior of earlier versions. With `scope = "geom"`, the functions also read the municipalities the grid reaches, so those cells hold every address inside them, and $P$ is computed from the addresses inside the grid.

The tables below show what each function does for each combination of `code_muni`, `scope` and, in `compute_lumi()`, `p_target`. "Given" means that `code_muni` is passed, with one code or several, and "omitted" means that it's left out. Whenever several municipalities are read, their addresses are pooled before anything is computed.

**`cnefe_counts()`**

| Units | `code_muni` | `scope` | Addresses read | Units on the outer edge | What to consider |
|:------|:------|:------|:--------------|:--------------|:--------------|
| H3 grid | given | `"muni"` (default) | Those of the municipalities in `code_muni` | Hold only the addresses of the requested municipalities | The fastest option. An address geocoded beyond the grid isn't counted, and a warning says how many there are |
| H3 grid | given | `"geom"` | Also those of the municipalities the grid reaches, listed in a message | Hold every address inside them | The CNEFE file of each neighbor is read in full |
| H3 grid | omitted | either | | | Error, since the grid is built from the boundaries of `code_muni` |
| Polygons | given | `"muni"` (default) | Those of the municipalities in `code_muni` | A polygon that extends beyond them gets only the part inside them | A warning reports how many of those addresses fall outside the polygons |
| Polygons | omitted | `"muni"` (default) | | | Error, which suggests passing `code_muni` or using `"geom"` |
| Polygons | given or omitted | `"geom"` | Those of the municipalities the polygons intersect, found from the 2022 IBGE boundaries and listed in a message. A given `code_muni` is ignored, with a message | Hold every address inside them | A polygon that touches a neighbor by a few meters makes the package read it too. The counts don't change, but the call is slower |

With polygons, in any of these cases, repeated features are dropped with a message, and overlapping polygons are reported, since the addresses in the overlap are counted in each of them.

**`compute_lumi()`**

The addresses read and the units on the outer edge are the same as in `cnefe_counts()`, and so are the errors. What changes is the $P$ that `bal` and `bgbi` use. The other four indices and `p_res` are computed within each unit and don't depend on $P$.

| Units | `code_muni` | `scope` | `p_target` | $P$ used by `bal` and `bgbi` | What to consider |
|:------|:------|:------|:------|:--------------|:--------------|
| H3 grid | given | `"muni"` (default) | `NULL` (default) | The share of every address of the municipalities in `code_muni`, which is the region when there are several | Adding a municipality changes `bal` and `bgbi` in every cell, not only near it |
| H3 grid | given | `"geom"` | `NULL` | The share of the addresses inside the cells of the grid, including those of the neighbors in the edge cells | $P$ describes the area covered by the grid rather than the municipalities requested |
| Polygons | given | `"muni"` (default) | `NULL` | The share of every address of the municipalities in `code_muni`, including those outside the polygons | The coverage warning says that those addresses are still part of $P$ |
| Polygons | given or omitted | `"geom"` | `NULL` | The share of the addresses inside the polygons, each counted once where polygons overlap | For polygons that cover only part of a city, $P$ is the share of those polygons alone |
| Any | any | any | a number in (0, 1) | `p_target` itself | `scope` still decides which addresses enter each unit. The same target gives comparable values across regions, and `bal` with a target is no longer the original Balance Index of Song et al. (2013) |

**`tracts_to_h3()`**

Here `code_muni` is always required, since the grid is built from it, and each dwelling is matched only to the census tracts of its own municipality.

| `code_muni` | `scope` | Tracts and dwellings used | Cells on the outer edge | What to consider |
|:------|:------|:--------------|:--------------|:--------------|
| given | `"muni"` (default) | Those of the municipalities in `code_muni` | Receive only the allocations of the requested municipalities | The fastest option |
| given | `"geom"` | Also the dwellings of the municipalities the grid reaches, and the tracts of those municipalities that have at least one dwelling inside the grid, with all their dwellings | Receive the allocation of every dwelling inside them | The result is the one a call listing the neighbors in `code_muni` would give, restricted to the cells of this grid. The CNEFE file of each neighbor is read in full, so the call is slower |
| omitted | either | | | Error |

**`tracts_to_polygon()`**

| `code_muni` | `scope` | Tracts and dwellings used | Polygons on the outer edge | What to consider |
|:------|:------|:--------------|:--------------|:--------------|
| given | `"muni"` (default) | Those of the municipalities in `code_muni` | A polygon that extends beyond them receives only the allocation of the requested municipalities | Stage 2 of the diagnostic report gives the share of allocated dwellings that fall inside the polygons |
| omitted | `"muni"` (default) | | | Error, which suggests passing `code_muni` or using `"geom"` |
| given or omitted | `"geom"` | Those of the municipalities the polygons intersect, even across states, listed in a message. A given `code_muni` is ignored, with a message | Receive the allocation of every dwelling inside them | As in `cnefe_counts()`, a polygon that touches a neighbor by a few meters makes the package read it too, without changing the values |

In both interpolation functions, the totals of separate calls add up, so they can be summed by cell or by polygon, but `avg_inc_resp` can't, because it's an average over the allocated dwellings.

On the tested example, the new subsection "Several municipalities at once" runs a call over Salvador and Lauro de Freitas every time the manuscript is rendered. The tests in `tests/testthat/test-multi-muni.R` use the referee's numbers on synthetic adjacent municipalities, on both backends. They check that both separate grids contain the shared cell, that the joint call returns it once with 20 private households and 51 other-use addresses, that its residential share is 20 / 71 while the mean of the separate shares is 0.5, that `bal` and `bgbi` are computed against the pooled $P$, and that the counts of the joint call equal the sums of the separate ones. Further tests cover a polygon that crosses the border, both interpolation functions, and a vector with a single code, which gives the same result as the scalar call.

The supplementary script `reproduce_h3_border_cells.R` still finds shared identifiers, as it should, because it builds each municipality's grid separately and those grids haven't changed. What changed is that users no longer need to combine them.

In the manuscript, the limitation, the loop and the sentence are removed from Section 6. Section 3 now says that every function accepts one or more codes, and the subsection on `cnefe_counts()` describes the rule for building the grid, including the neighboring cells. A new subsection of Section 4, "Several municipalities at once", covers the four functions, with a table of what each of them reads under each value of `scope` and a paragraph on $P$ and `p_target`. Since the subsections of the template aren't numbered, the manuscript now names them in its cross-references, and this document does the same.

# Comment 2: Correct the direction of the construction-site interpretation

> Section 4.3, p. 9 (source lines 720–728), says excluding type 7 will "understate the residential share those areas are heading towards" if construction ends up in the same proportions as existing addresses. This condition does not establish the direction of change. If it means the citywide proportions, an area's share can rise or fall depending on its starting composition. For example, an area with 90 private-household records among 100 eligible records has a share of 90%. Reclassifying ten construction records as eight private households and two other uses gives `98 / 110 = 89.1%`, a decrease despite the additions being mostly residential. If it means the existing local proportions, the share is unchanged. Please clarify which proportions are meant and correct the direction claim. The type-7 filtering fix is verified; this request concerns its interpretation and needs only a wording correction.

**Response:** **Accepted. The paragraph now states both readings and drops the direction claim.**

The referee's example shows the problem well. We had in mind the municipality's proportions, where private households are the large majority, and we took that to mean the residential share could only rise. But the share moves toward the municipal value, so it rises only where the area starts below it. The paragraph in the subsection on `compute_lumi()` now reads:

> Type 7 addresses are left out because a building under construction or renovation describes a transitional state rather than a realized use, so the indices describe each area as it is now. The exclusion has no fixed direction. If these buildings end up in the same proportions as the area's existing addresses, the residential share doesn't change. If they follow the municipality's overall proportions instead, the share moves toward the municipal value, rising where the area is less residential than the municipality and falling where it is more so. In both cases the effect grows with the share of type 7 addresses in the area.

# Comment 3: Finish cleanup of connections and uncached files

> In `R/utils-internal.R`, lines 1201–1223, `.duckdb_connect()` opens the connection, applies user configuration, and only then registers disconnection. An invalid setting or malformed configuration can fail before cleanup is registered. Retained-connection probes confirmed that the connection remained valid after those errors; normal-return and later-error controls closed correctly. Please register guarded cleanup immediately after connection creation, before applying configuration or loading extensions, and test these error paths.
>
> With `cache = FALSE`, the R paths of `cnefe_counts()` and `compute_lumi()` retrieve the municipal data twice: once before selecting the backend and again through `read_cnefe()`. For example, `R/cnefe_counts.R` retrieves at line 176 but calls the reader without passing that file at line 279. Reuse the retrieved path. In the controlled checks, counts and indices left one temporary Gzip file after return on either backend, while interpolation left a temporary tract Parquet. Please ensure each function deletes the temporary files it owns on success and error. This is needed to fulfil the deletion-on-exit promise on p. 4 (source lines 371–372).
>
> The supplementary scripts `reproduce_connection_cleanup.R` and `reproduce_uncached_files.R` provide reproducible examples. The first exercises the shared connection helper without mocks. The second replaces only downloads with tiny synthetic inputs and exercises the real `cnefe_counts()` and `tracts_to_polygon()` functions.
>
> Please add focused tests of these resource-handling fixes through the package functions, so later changes do not accidentally reintroduce the failures.

**Response:** **Accepted in full.**

We confirmed both problems, and they mean two statements from the first round were only partly true. Our response to R1.12 and R2.C3 said that cleanup was registered "immediately after `dbConnect()` returns, before any extension load can fail", but the user configuration was applied before it. And the manuscript promised that with `cache = FALSE` the data "is removed when the function exits", which wasn't the case for the files the referee lists. Both bugs are also in version 0.3.0 on CRAN, and 0.4.0 will fix them.

- **Connections.** `.duckdb_connect()` now registers the guarded disconnection right after the connection is created, before the user configuration is applied and before any extension is loaded.
- **The second download.** On the R backend, `cnefe_counts()` and `compute_lumi()` now pass the file they already retrieved to `read_cnefe(file = ...)`, so the municipality is downloaded once.
- **Temporary files.** Each function now registers the deletion of the temporary files it creates as soon as they exist, both the CNEFE file and the census tract Parquet, so they are removed when the function returns or fails. The deletion runs after the connection is closed, because Windows won't delete a file that DuckDB still holds open.
The tests are in `tests/testthat/test-cleanup.R`. They mock only the downloads and go through the exported functions. They check that `cnefe_counts()` and `compute_lumi()` download once and leave no file on either backend, that the file is deleted when the function fails partway through, that `tracts_to_polygon()` leaves neither the CNEFE file nor the tract Parquet behind, and that an invalid configuration closes the connection, both through the helper and inside `cnefe_counts()`. Seven of the eight tests were written for this comment, and all seven fail on the reviewed commit. The eighth covers the per-municipality tract read added in this round. Both supplementary scripts now fail their `stopifnot()` checks, as they should once the defects are fixed.

The deletion-on-exit sentence in Section 3 is now accurate, so it stays as it was.

# Corrections to our first-round response

Besides the two statements under Comment 3, a few points in our first-round response no longer hold. We list them here so the referee doesn't have to find them.

- **R2.5 (single-municipality scope).** We described iterating over municipalities as the way to work around the limitation, with two caveats, and the first caveat was the one the referee found to be wrong in Comment 1. The workaround is no longer needed, and the manuscript no longer presents it. The `tracts_to` article on the package website now says that binding separate results gives the right answer only when every polygon lies inside one municipality.
- **R2.3 (scope of $P$).** We argued that $P$ should stay citywide when `polygon` is supplied, and that's still the default. With several municipalities, though, "the city" becomes the set of municipalities requested, and under `scope = "geom"` the edge cells also hold addresses from municipalities outside that set. Computing $P$ from every address of the requested municipalities would then leave out addresses that are in the cells, so under `scope = "geom"` $P$ is computed from the addresses inside the output geometries. This is an option, not the default, and the documentation says it measures mix relative to the area covered rather than relative to the city, as we put it in the first round. The subsection on `compute_lumi()` now says "by default" where it said "always".
- **R1.11 (the `zipfs` extension).** We wrote that `zipfs` was still loaded on demand for a ZIP, from an older cache or supplied by the user. In fact neither case reaches it. The cache is always a gzipped CSV, and a ZIP passed to `read_cnefe(file = ...)` is read through `utils::unzip()` and Arrow. The package doesn't use `zipfs`, and the sentence is removed from Section 3.
- **R1.8b (grid sizes).** We reported grids of 550 cells for Lauro de Freitas and 2651 for Fortaleza at resolution 9. The boundaries are now read at full resolution instead of the simplified geobr version, so those grids have 547 and 2648 cells. The difference is at the border and doesn't change any conclusion.
- **Benchmark figures.** The numbers in Section 5 and in the abstract now come from the benchmark run on the current version. DuckDB's advantage on São Paulo is now above twentyfold, where we had reported sixteenfold. The DuckDB version also changed between the two runs, so we don't attribute the difference to the package alone.

# Smaller changes to the manuscript

While revising, we also made a few changes that no comment asked for.

- Address type 7 is now described as "under construction or renovation" throughout, following the IBGE label (*Edificação em construção ou reforma*). The text said "under construction" in some places.
- The `duckdb` R package is cited where it first appears, in the Introduction.
- The caption of the table of interpolation variables showed raw LaTeX markup in the PDF, and it's fixed.
- Code examples call the functions without the `cnefetools::` prefix throughout.
- Sentences that referred to the behavior of earlier versions of the package were rewritten, since the article is the reader's first contact with it.

We hope these changes address the referee's comments, and we thank them again for the time they put into both rounds.

Sincerely,

Jorge Ubirajara Pedreira Junior and Bruno Henrique Mioto Stabile
